articles.title: She spent decades as an FBI agent and this is the case she could not let go
articles.summary: Jane Collins had all but given up on seeing Michael Donovan and Richard Moore face justice. Then they were charged with stealing from a mass-shooter’s brother.
articles.body:
Jane Collins had spent 30 years as an FBI agent, but there was one case that haunted her long after retirement.

Michael Donovan was a fraudster, former minister and multimillionaire she had pursued for years, and even in her retirement she could not escape him.

He was regularly featured in the news and on the radio, appearing as a spokesperson for a number of causes, from migrant rights to anti-racism and justice reform.

He and his husband, Richard Moore, lived about an hour's drive from her, in Augusta County, Virginia, on the edge of the Appalachian Mountains.

Together they owned a business, Libre by Nexus, which had made more than $200m (£152m) from migrants seeking release from US immigrant detention centres - but it was a scam, government regulators said.

To Collins, they were the ones who got away.

She had investigated Nexus from 2016 until her retirement from the FBI in 2021. But the only federal criminal charges either faced - after almost six years of her investigation - was a tax charge against Moore.

So when Collins left the bureau, there were still a few strands left of her investigation that she could not let go - like the case of Zach Cruz, the brother of the man who killed 17 people in Parkland, Florida.

They had fronted his $500,000 bail bond, personally picked him up from jail, given him somewhere to stay, and made media appearances on his behalf.

Investigators later found they also took $400,000 from him, proceeds from his late mother's life insurance. Last month, the pair were found guilty of stealing it - with Collins playing a key role as a witness during the trial.

Collins told the BBC in her only interview about the case that she saw it as her final chance to face them in court.

"It means something when people are held to account," she said.

Collins says she was still a young girl when she first thought about joining the FBI.

"I've always been very interested in justice, making things right, and I think all of those things just fell into place," the 64-year-old recalls from her home in Charlottesville, Virginia, where a picture of her late golden retriever named Yogi hangs on the wall and a vintage car is parked in the driveway.

She was accepted to Quantico, the FBI training academy, soon after finishing university, and began to climb the ladder at the bureau, conducting surveillance on suspected Russian spies and crack dealers. In the late 1990s, she began working more on white-collar crimes, which really excited her - "much to my surprise," she adds. What she liked about these cases was the paper trail, and the way they presented themselves as puzzles to solve.

"There's a lot more in those cases that are concrete. As we say, documents don't lie," she says. "It was more challenging."

It also changed her perspective on crime, and victims. Although there was no trail of blood, there was an undeniable ripple from the fraud to the people and families hurt by it.

"People getting defrauded of money, some people their life savings," she explains. "There's a lot of psychological issues that go with that for a victim. They have been duped, so they're very hard on themselves."

Weeks after his older brother gunned down 14 students and three staff members at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Zachary Cruz went to the campus to "reflect on the school shooting and soak it all in".

But when police found him there skateboarding, they arrested the then 18-year-old, charged him with trespassing and put him in jail. On the heels of his brother's massacre, a judge set his bail at $500,000.

His friend called Nexus, looking for help to get him out. But Donovan and Moore did more than that - not only did they pay his bail, but they picked Cruz up from jail and took him to a hotel room.

Cruz later told the court that when he met them for the first time, it felt "like a movie".

During dinner that first night, the couple asked Cruz if he wanted to move to Virginia and work for Nexus.

The Florida judge overseeing his probation called it a "wonderful opportunity".

Soon he was living with them, and sharing in their media spotlight. Donovan and Moore accompanied him on interviews where the young man spoke about trying to understand his brother's crimes.

The couple even helped produce a short-lived online reality show called "Being Zach Cruz", which chronicled what it's like to be the brother of a famous killer.

According to Moore and Donovan, in an interview with the BBC in 2022, Cruz had become part of their family. They called him their "son" and said they had spent lavishly on his pursuit of a skateboarding career.

But they were deeply in debt, fighting off creditors - and the IRS. And through it all, Collins was doggedly on their tail.

Donovan and Moore had spent their wealth extravagantly - a fleet of luxury vehicles, a $500,000 wedding and a million-dollar self-published book titled Not Free America: What Your Government Doesn't Want You to Know.

But they owed millions to several state insurance boards, which had fined them for operating an unlicensed bond company. They owed a former business partner, RLI Insurance, millions for their failure to pay back bail that was lost when clients skipped court. And Moore owed more than $3m to the IRS.

Prosecutors alleged it was this tax debt that spurred Moore and Donovan to dupe Cruz out of his inheritance. Donovan declined an interview, through his attorney.

Collins initially focused her investigation on Libre by Nexus, and whether the company had broken any laws.

But her case took a turn when she received a tip that Donovan and Moore may be personally exploiting Cruz.

Bank records showed that $428,000 - the insurance money Cruz was entitled to after his mother died - was transferred into a joint account held by Cruz and Moore, and then into Moore's personal account, in 2019, according to the county's search warrant.

Collins tried to interview Cruz, who was still living with Moore and Donovan.

Driving up to their house one evening, Collins says she saw an armed security guard stationed outside, while barricades blocked the entrance to the front door and driveway.

"People can't easily come and go," she thought to herself. Cruz never came to the door.

Since 2016, Collins had been working on the case in conjunction with the Internal Revenue Service and Homeland Security Investigations, which oversees immigration law. The agencies were investigating whether Nexus defrauded people and brought migrants illegally to work for their company, as well as the allegations involving Cruz's insurance money and tax fraud.

But by the time she was due to retire, the federal prosecutor in charge of the case had narrowed the focus to just tax fraud, which he passed onto another prosecutor.

Ultimately, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau - a federal agency with the power to bring civil, but not criminal, cases to court - took legal action against Nexus, leading to an $811m judgement against the company.

The agency provides a much-needed service, helping to pursue corporations when other avenues have failed, said Ted Mermin, executive director of the Berkeley Center for Consumer Law & Economic Justice.

To bring a criminal case, "you have to show that beyond a shadow of a doubt they violated the law", he said.

A civil case, on the other hand, only needs to show that it is more likely than not that they violated the law.

Meanwhile, Collins was running up against the clock: the FBI has a mandatory retirement age of 57, and she had already been extended. She retired in the summer of 2021 at the age of 59.

A few months later, Cruz, Donovan and Moore sued her, alleging she had "conspired to create a fake 'joint investigation'" with a local agency, and that her career was "cut short after she violated department policies and/or laws in connection with her rogue investigation".

The bureau's attorney repudiated those claims, and a federal judge dismissed the case. The lawsuit did little to dissuade Collins, who brushed it off as "frivolous".

"I was not intimidated by them," she told the BBC. Through his attorney, Donovan declined the BBC's request for comment. Moore, who is serving a seven-year prison sentence for filing a fraudulent Nexus tax return, did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Before she left the bureau, Collins sat down with her bosses and the agent assigned to take the case over from her, she said. She still had hope that it would be prosecuted.

But more than a year went by, and there were no charges.

It seemed, at least for a while, that her case was finished. Then, in October 2022, local police and Virginia State Police stormed Moore and Donovan's home in Fishersville, and their offices in Verona.

It was not the feds, as Collins had hoped. But this was still a chance at holding the men to account.

They seized laptops, mobile phones, body cameras and thumb drives. Donovan and Moore were arrested and charged, and then released on bail.

Evidence of the raid was still clear in the shattered glass of the front door, when the BBC went to Nexus offices to interview the couple several days after police stormed the property.

In the interview, Donovan and Moore said they had not taken advantage of Cruz and had done nothing wrong.

Zach, who was still living with them at the time, told the BBC he had spent all his inheritance willingly. But he is no longer living with the couple, and appeared as a witness for the prosecution during the trial.

After Collins retired from the bureau in 2021, she began working for a state agency. She plans to retire for good in a few years, when she hopes to spend more time with her husband and three children and travel around the world.

Looking back, she thinks of this chapter at the end of her career in federal law enforcement as discouraging. She had wanted to declare "case closed" years ago.

"I enjoyed my career immensely. I wouldn't trade it. I felt like I made a big difference in a lot of ways," she says. "But this case, it caused me a lot of frustration."

Still, she says, she feels grateful that someone did take this case on.

When she heard the jury had convicted them on all counts, she thought: "Finally, justice".

"It had been a long time coming," she said. "But we needed to wait until the house of cards fell down."

Couple ‘exploited’ Parkland school gunman's brother

They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop

articles.title: BJP-SAD alliance: Captain Amarinder missing from match-making moment
articles.summary: Capt Amarinder Singh was absent as SAD and BJP formally reunited in Delhi, despite long backing the alliance for Punjab’s 2027 polls amid BJP state-level pushback.
articles.body: Chandigarh: Former Punjab chief minister and senior BJP functionary Capt Amarinder Singh was conspicuously absent from the dais in New Delhi on Tuesday as SAD and BJP formally reunited — an alliance Amarinder had long championed, arguing BJP could not form a govt on its own in Punjab in 2027.Amarinder was unavailable for comment by phone but his long-time media aide and former press secretary, Vimal Sumbly, flagged it on X: “Conspicuous absence of @captamarinder from the dais! He was the staunch votary of alliance between @BJP4India and @AkaliDal_, when BJP national leadership would claim to go solo. But he was not present today. Strange!”The absence stood out given Amarinder’s central role in BJP’s Punjab strategy since the 2022 state elections, when his Punjab Lok Congress contested alongside BJP and Sukhdev Singh Dhindsa’s SAD (Sanyukt), with BJP winning two seats.In a Dec 2025 interview with an online news channel, Amarinder warned that without a regional partner holding sway over Sikh and rural voters, BJP faced a bleak choice: “Politically, we will have to stitch an alliance. Else, you will have to wait for two-three elections to strengthen the ground position in villages and cities.”In that interview, Amarinder also detailed how pre-poll talks collapsed ahead of the 2024 Lok Sabha elections. He said discussions with SAD president Sukhbir Singh Badal had neared an understanding for BJP to contest four seats in Punjab and one in Chandigarh. However, Badal subsequently phoned Amit Shah to offer only three Punjab seats, prompting Shah to instruct then-BJP president JP Nadda to field candidates in all constituencies, Amarinder said.While Amarinder viewed the 2027 assembly polls as a vital second chance to revive the partnership, his blunt assessment drew pushback from state BJP leaders at the time. Then state working president Ashwani Sharma dismissed Amarinder’s remarks as a “personal opinion”, insisting the party was preparing to contest all 117 seats, while former minister Surjit Jyani stressed that alliance decisions rested solely with the central leadership.Former Punjab BJP president Sunil Jakhar had similarly backed a tie-up, arguing a moderate Akali Dal was essential for Punjab’s political and social balance. Senior Akali leader Balwinder Singh Bhunder had also welcomed Amarinder’s remarks as factual, though he cautioned that any pact required New Delhi to address Punjab’s broader concerns and SAD’s demands beyond mere seat-sharing.A week before Tuesday’s announcement, Amarinder’s presence at the Nov 16 launch of Congress parliamentary party chairperson Sonia Gandhi’s memoir in Delhi had triggered a buzz in Punjab politics. articles.summary: At least 20 people remained hostage at a supermarket in Colombia's Cartagena on Tuesday by armed men, following a failed attempt to hijack an armoured
articles.body: At least 20 people remained hostage at a supermarket in Colombia's Cartagena on Tuesday by armed men, following a failed attempt to hijack an armoured cash van, President Abelardo De La Espriella and national police said.The hostage-takers had released 10 people from the store, which belongs to the Exito chain, Reuters reported.The armed men reportedly took the hostages after police responded to their failed attempt to intercept an armoured vehicle carrying cash from a shopping mall, De La Espriella said. They subsequently barricaded themselves inside the supermarket in Cartagena's La Castellana neighbourhood.Images shared on social media earlier on Tuesday appeared to show people kneeling against the supermarket's windows with their hands seemingly tied. However, they couldn’t be verified.Heavily armed military personnel and police officers were deployed outside the store. Police said on social media that all available human, technological and specialised resources had been mobilised to protect those still inside and secure their safe release."All of our human, technological, and specialised resources are deployed, under interagency coordination, to protect the citizens who remain inside the store and secure their safe release," the police said, as per Reuters.Authorities did not immediately disclose the identities of the hostage-takers or those being held. De La Espriella assured the public that the hostages would be freed."I guarantee the Colombian people that we will free those people," he said during a visit to Villavicencio, where an overnight car bombing had taken place. The government blamed the bombing on a group of dissidents from the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) who rejected the 2016 peace agreement.The Exito chain said the safety and protection of people was its priority and that authorities were handling the situation at its Cartagena store.Meanwhile, Cartagena's Rafael Nunez airport resumed flight arrivals after a suspension of around 45 minutes. articles.title: UK warns companies of potential Russian sabotage threat
articles.summary: Britain’s Defence Ministry and security service warn of the threat in unusual public announcement.
articles.body:
Britain’s Defence Ministry and the country’s security service, known as MI5, are warning companies that support Ukraine’s military that they may face attempted sabotage from Russia.

“If your organisation supports military procurement or supplies equipment to Ukraine’s armed forces, it could be a target,” the Ministry of Defence and the National Protective Security Authority said in an unusual public announcement on Tuesday.

“This activity is typically characterised by the use of proxy actors employing low-sophistication sabotage methodologies, such as arson,” the warning said, urging companies to take action against security threats posed by what they described as operatives acting for Russia.

Russia’s embassy in London denied such claims in a statement and said: “Russia has no plans, reasons or intentions to attack the UK.”

It also accused Ukraine of carrying out sabotage to “put the blame on Russia and extort more money from western governments”, something Kyiv has repeatedly denied.

Since the Ukraine war started and Britain became one of Kyiv’s key supporters, London has accused Russia of being behind a number of spying and sabotage plots.

Last year, three British men were convicted for an arson attack on a warehouse storing Starlink satellite equipment bound for Ukraine, which prosecutors said was carried out by Russian military intelligence agents.

In September, a man was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service after alleged contact with Russian military spies.

On Sunday, Estonia said it would close all its border crossing points with Russia following a suspected sabotage attack on an Estonian defence company, while last week the Norwegian security service said it expected Russian intelligence to carry out sabotage attacks in Norway in the coming year.

Britain’s Ministry of Defence said it was holding closed-door security briefings with leaders from the critical national infrastructure and defence sectors over the next two days to advise on security.

“Recent sabotage attempts right across Europe demonstrate the seriousness of the threats we face,” Security Minister Dan Jarvis said.

“It’s truly shameful that actors are seeking to disrupt our way of life and that of our allies, especially targeting organisations doing vital work in support of Ukraine.”

articles.title: Phone spying to missiles: Why India-Israel strategic ties go beyond Modi
articles.summary: The opposition Congress party calls Israel’s war on Gaza a genocide, but its leader still wants strong ties with Israel.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India – For the past three years, India’s main opposition party, the Indian National Congress, has frequently criticised Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government for its refusal to condemn Israel’s war on Gaza, acknowledging it as a genocide.

Yet when asked about his position on Israel in an interview last week, the party’s de facto leader, Rahul Gandhi, was more nuanced. He condemned Israel’s genocidal war but added: “I support a strong relationship with Israel. We have strategic interests, including buying the best weapons for our armed forces.”

Those comments sparked a backlash from some of the Congress party’s allies, including left parties. But analysts said they reflect the depth of a strategic partnership that, while controversial, is seen as critical by both India and Israel. It’s a relationship that has grown dramatically under Modi but extends beyond his Hindu majoritarian Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government and is one that is likely to outlast its rule.

From weapons and surveillance to policing and hacking, India has increasingly turned to Israel as a vital partner and source of expertise, binding the two countries in ways that are hard to disentangle even if the political winds shift in either nation.

This month, an investigation by the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), a nonprofit, found that Home Minister Amit Shah had waived India’s own rules to allow the purchase of phone-hacking technology from Israel.

Indians have been here before. In 2019, WhatsApp disclosed that Pegasus spyware , developed by Israel’s NSO Group, had been used to target Indian journalists and human rights defenders. Amnesty International later confirmed infections on the phones of journalists Siddharth Varadarajan and Anand Mangnale. The government denied unauthorised surveillance.

Together, the cases point to a dependency, analysts said. India’s cooperation with Israel “has always involved examining and exploring Israeli methods for intelligence gathering, border management and controlling dissent”, author Azad Essa told Al Jazeera.

“It was only a matter of time before Israeli products or methods would be used against Indians themselves, including farmers,” added Essa, author of Hostile Homelands, a book on the burgeoning alliance between India and Israel. Essa is also the author of an upcoming book, The Architecture of Complicity: How India Helped Israel Conduct a Genocide, scheduled for publication in January 2027.

In Haryana, Delhi’s neighbouring state, the government there spent six years trying to replicate Israeli police and army tactics, and in February 2024, state police used drones to fire tear gas at farmers marching towards Delhi.

The phone tools are the newest layer of a relationship that runs deep into India’s defence industry. Since 2014, India has become Israel’s most reliable arms buyer, taking about 37 percent of its exports.

At the centre of this relationship sits the Adani Group, led by billionaire Gautam Adani, widely seen as a close Modi associate. In 2016, the Indian conglomerate formed a joint venture with Israel’s Elbit Systems to make Hermes 900 drones in Hyderabad, the first such facility outside Israel. Since 2020, Adani has held a 51 percent stake in BLR Systems, which makes Negev machinegun parts with Israel Weapon Industries. In January 2023, Adani and Israel’s Gadot completed the $1.15bn purchase of Haifa’s port, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attended the handover.

Essa says India “is increasingly becoming a manufacturing and supply base for Israeli companies”.

Ashutosh Singh, an independent researcher in New Delhi who studies Palestine and the Middle East, agreed, calling Hyderabad the best example of Indian capital embedded in Israel’s military infrastructure built “in the garb” of the Make in India initiative, a programme meant to indigenise manufacturing.

Nicolas Blarel, an associate professor of international relations at Leiden University in the Netherlands, added a note of caution. What happens in Hyderabad is “mostly late assembly” of Israeli-designed drones, he told Al Jazeera, and it is “not clear how much technology has been actually completely shared”. But he noted that deliveries were made to Israel in late 2023 and early 2024 when some of those drone models were being used for the genocide in Gaza.

Amnesty International’s “Made in India” report, published on July 30, documented 2,596 shipments of weapons, ammunition and military components from Indian firms to Israel from October 7, 2023, to November 30, 2025, referring to a period that began with the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel that served as the trigger for the assault on Gaza.

It named nine companies, three of them wholly owned by India’s Ministry of Defence, and concluded that the Indian state itself was transferring weapons whenever those firms export. Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the next day that India had a “robust” legal framework for strategic trade without addressing the allegations.

Ask analysts why India keeps buying from Israel, and the answer is less about technology than about what Israel does not demand in return.

Kabir Taneja of the Observer Research Foundation think tank said defence carries almost the entire relationship. A country that sells India a Western platform may refuse to share the source code needed to fit an Indian-built missile on it. Israel has been willing to bridge those gaps, for instance by fitting early-warning radars to a Russian Il-76 aircraft.

“Israel is that Walmart of defence technologies that you can just go and purchase without any terms and conditions that stop you from using these technologies in whatever manner is required,” Taneja told Al Jazeera.

He contrasted Israeli drones, which India deploys along its front with Pakistan, with the MQ-9s bought from the United States, which come unarmed and with restrictions on their use.

Blarel traced that trust to the 1999 Kargil War with Pakistan when other suppliers imposed embargoes after India’s nuclear tests but Israel kept supplying spare parts and ammunition. Israel “has not really cared for embargoes”, he said, and it has attached “no conditions”, something “both Congress and the BJP have noted”.

It also supplies technology the West “has always been more reluctant to supply”, and its systems work with Russian-origin equipment, which makes up much of India’s arsenal. Israeli firms, he said, “have been more willing to share technology and to work together” with Indian companies.

That matters because New Delhi now wants to build, not just buy. Taneja said India increasingly tells manufacturers that if they want to sell, they must indigenise a good chunk of production. The Hyderabad plant feeds that push, he said, while for the Israeli side, it is a commercial venture: “If the commercial part does not work, they will not come.” Israel’s appeal, in other words, is that it lets India buy now and localise later.

Does ideology drive the relationship? Experts are split.

Essa said ideology and strategy cannot be separated. “The relationship is both ideological and strategic,” he said. “Both states present themselves as civilisational states facing an existential crisis, often revolving around the idea of being besieged by Muslims. Much of this is underpinned by the kinship between Hindutva and Zionism.”

Hindutva is the Hindu majoritarian ideology of the BJP and its ideological parent, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS). The RSS seeks to turn India, constitutionally a secular republic, into a Hindu state.

Netanyahu has made a similar point from the other side. “We have problems of delegitimisation in the world, but not in India,” he said at a conference in the occupied West Bank in May. “There is tremendous love for Israel there, … truly tremendous. I think I have more followers from India than from anywhere else.”

Taneja saw none of that. The closeness is “at the base level of things very transactional”, he said, and driven by a country surrounded by security threats. If France offers the same, “I don’t think India will discriminate.”

Blarel sits in between. There is “a basis” for the ideological argument, he said, because RSS founders VD Savarkar and MS Golwalkar cited Israel as a model although they also admired Nazi Germany, which he called “an opportunistic understanding of these models”. Still, Modi’s personal affinity with Netanyahu is “not hidden”.

Salman Khurshid, a senior Congress leader and former Indian external affairs minister, said the government has never said which it is. Relying on Israel for defence “is understandable”, he said, but the country has not been told that Modi’s embrace comes from “some ideological affinity”.

India’s strategic relationship with and reliance on Israel did not begin with Modi. India voted against the United Nations Partition Plan for Palestine in 1947 and against Israel’s UN admission in 1949 yet recognised Israel in 1950, without embassies, accepting only an Israeli consul in Bombay for more than four decades.

Behind that diplomatic distance, help flowed in wartime. When China attacked India in 1962, Israel secretly supplied mortars and Uzi submachine guns. According to an Israeli archive document, New Delhi asked that they arrive on ships not flying the Israeli flag, and Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion refused.

In 1965 after the US and Britain halted arms to India and Pakistan during the war between the South Asian neighbours, Israel supplied mortars to New Delhi. In 1971, it diverted weapons meant for Iran, then ruled by Shah Reza Pahlavi, to India, which was fighting another war with Pakistan.

Essa said Israel’s Mossad intelligence service worked with the Research and Analysis Wing, India’s external intelligence agency, from the late 1960s and India later studied the fence on Israel’s border with Lebanon to inform fencing in India-administered Kashmir.

All the while, India championed the Palestinian cause. It was the first non-Arab state to recognise the Palestine Liberation Organization in 1974 and recognised the State of Palestine in 1988. Full diplomatic relations with Israel came only in 1992 when the Congress party was in power and after the Soviet Union’s collapse forced India to reassess its position in the world.

The BJP-led government under then-Prime Minister Atal Behari Vajpayee, which took office in the late 1990s, continued buying Israeli missiles and early-warning aircraft and began discussing coproduction. When the Congress party returned to power in 2004, it took ties to their next stage: A $350m deal in 2006 to develop the Barak-8 missile defence system moved the partnership from buying to codevelopment. “The ideological ties developed under Modi were informed by the relations built by previous governments, including Congress-led governments,” Essa said.

What changed after Modi became prime minister was the visibility of the relationship. Earlier governments took Israeli weapons while asking for unmarked ships and secret visits. After 2014, the cover came off.

During Israel’s Gaza offensive in July and August 2014, Modi’s government refused to let the upper house of the Indian Parliament adopt a resolution condemning Israel. In 2015, India abstained for the first time at the UN Human Rights Council on a resolution seeking accountability for that offensive and did so again in 2016. In 2017, Modi became the first Indian prime minister to visit Israel. He returned in February 2026, days before Israel and the US attacked Iran. In September 2024, India’s Supreme Court declined to hear a petition to halt arms exports to Israel, saying foreign policy was outside its jurisdiction.

Blarel said India’s stance on Palestine, once “very clear since the 1970s”, has become “a little bit more unpredictable”, which he said suited the BJP. Middle Eastern diplomats “don’t really understand” where it stands, he said, a position “lacking in moral clarity”. Taneja disagreed that anything fundamental has changed. India continues to insist on a two-state solution, he said, and “we have done what we were supposed to do.”

But Essa pointed to how India has sent Israel arms during the latest war on Gaza, did not join the genocide case against Israel before the International Court of Justice, did not endorse an arms embargo on Israel and cracked down on pro-Palestinian protests at home. “These actions speak louder than India’s supposed policies towards Palestine,” he said.

Taneja said the change in tone also reflects India’s economic weight. In the 1960s, he said, India was economically small, and the cost of upsetting other powers was high. Today, as an economy of about $4 trillion with large requirements to protect its trade and security, it can absorb the pushback, and it will seek security from whichever partners offer it, including Israel, he said.

For critics, the question is accountability. A UN commission of inquiry found in June that at least 20,179 Palestinian children were killed in two years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and urged states to halt arms transfers that “have involved or could involve” genocide, a report Israel rejected in its entirety.

Asked whether the Indian state and its companies are complicit in war crimes in Gaza, Essa answered: “I believe so.” India “cannot claim to have been unaware”, he said. Singh said any country materially providing Israel with tools for genocide is complicit.

As for the opposition Congress, Khurshid did not dispute reports that some states ruled by the party had also bought Israeli phone-extraction tools. He said there must be “guardrails” and “those limits, I’m afraid, are not apparent in the dealings that the government of India has with them.”

But, he acknowledged, “this is not a perfect world.”

articles.title: Political tensions, AI-powered attacks to dominate APAC cyber threat landscape in 2027: Kaspersky
articles.summary: Geopolitical rivalries, regional conflicts and the growing use of artificial intelligence by cybercriminals are expected to play a major role in shaping
articles.body: Geopolitical rivalries, regional conflicts and the growing use of artificial intelligence by cybercriminals are expected to play a major role in shaping the Asia-Pacific (APAC) cybersecurity landscape in 2027, according to Kaspersky’s Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT). The cybersecurity company said that while rapid advances in AI will continue to influence cyberattacks, persistent political and regional tensions across APAC are likely to remain the most significant drivers of advanced persistent threat (APT) activity next year. The region has increasingly become a target for state-linked cyber groups seeking diplomatic, strategic and financial gains, with sectors such as aviation, finance and government infrastructure frequently in the crosshairs.Geopolitical tensions to fuel cyber espionageSergey Lozhkin, Head of Kaspersky's Research Center for the Asia-Pacific and Middle East, Türkiye and Africa regions, said APAC's position as both a hub of digital transformation and a region marked by geopolitical tensions makes it a prime target for sophisticated cyber operations.According to Kaspersky, organisations across both the public and private sectors should prepare for continued cyber espionage campaigns targeting defence, telecommunications and critical infrastructure. The company also warned that territorial disputes and political instability in parts of the region could lead to an increase in hacktivist campaigns and targeted phishing attacks aimed at influencing public opinion and local narratives.AI-powered cyberattacks expected to become more sophisticatedKaspersky researchers expect AI weaponisation to mature significantly in 2027, enabling attackers to automate larger portions of the cyber kill chain. Threat actors are likely to deploy AI-powered systems capable of conducting reconnaissance, identifying vulnerabilities and launching intrusions with minimal human intervention.The company said the time between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation could shrink to just a few days, providing attackers with a faster path to compromise systems. Small and medium-sized businesses are expected to become increasingly attractive targets due to limited cybersecurity resources, while larger enterprises may face more stealthy and difficult-to-detect attacks.Kaspersky also predicts that advanced threat groups will increasingly leverage open-source large language models to generate spear-phishing campaigns, create exploit code and conduct deepfake-enabled social engineering attacks targeting senior executives and government officials.India's elections and local supply chains in focusFor India, Kaspersky believes several domestic developments could significantly influence cyber threats in 2027. Among them are upcoming state elections in Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Uttarakhand, Goa, Manipur, Gujarat and Himachal Pradesh, along with the Presidential election scheduled for July.Saurabh Sharma, Lead Security Researcher at Kaspersky GReAT, said these political events could become focal points for cyber operations involving deepfakes, phishing campaigns and influence operations targeting political parties and campaign staff.The company also highlighted risks emerging from India's expanding "Make in India" manufacturing ecosystem. As more domestic suppliers, vendors and manufacturers become integrated into strategic industries such as defence, electronics and telecommunications, attackers may increasingly target supply chains to gain access to critical systems.According to Sharma, threat actors are expected to focus on compromising open-source software components, firmware updates and trusted software-as-a-service platforms used by Indian organisations, particularly those operated by smaller Tier-2 and Tier-3 vendors with weaker cybersecurity controls.Post-quantum transition may attract nation-state actorsKaspersky further warned that India's early adoption of post-quantum cryptography could draw the attention of nation-state-backed threat groups.As critical infrastructure organisations begin piloting post-quantum algorithms, attackers may intensify "harvest now, decrypt later" operations, in which encrypted information is stolen today with the expectation that future quantum computing capabilities could eventually unlock the data.The company said current encryption standards such as RSA and ECC remain widely used across digital communications, but advances in quantum computing have prompted governments and enterprises worldwide to prepare for cryptographic migration.Regulatory changes may create new targetsThe report also noted that increasing regulatory requirements and data localisation mandates could reshape India's cyber risk environment. Regulations such as the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA) are prompting organisations to store more sensitive information locally, creating larger repositories of valuable data that may attract nation-state adversaries.Sharma said businesses should not assume regulatory compliance alone will protect them from sophisticated attacks. Instead, organisations need to focus on identifying where critical data resides, implementing strong encryption and access controls, and monitoring network traffic for potential data exfiltration attempts.Security measures recommendedTo mitigate evolving cyber threats, Kaspersky urged organisations to maintain robust patch management practices, deploy advanced threat detection and incident response technologies, and invest in regular cybersecurity awareness training.The company noted that spear-phishing remains one of the most common entry points for APT campaigns, making employee education a critical layer of defence against increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Cornwall Christmas market cancels all bookings after AI backlash
articles.summary: Visitors and stallholders say the event did not match the promotional AI pictures.
articles.body:
The organisers of a Christmas market have cancelled all bookings and promised to refund ticket-holders following a backlash to AI-generated promotional materials.

David Rowland, who produced the images for Kernow Christmas Market in Pool, Cornwall, said claims they did not match reality were a "lesson learned".

Images showed rows of stalls beneath Christmas decorations, fairy lights and festive displays for the event last weekend. But photographs taken by visitors showed a mostly empty hall with only a handful of traders, little Christmas decoration and buckets on the floor collecting water from a leaking roof.

Rowlands Attractions said it was "gutted" things "didn't go as planned".

It said: "The criticism we have faced and the words that have been seen on social media and across the news make us look at the world slightly differently.

"Kindness and compassion goes out of the window so easily to knock something that people don't care to understand the full story of."

The company added: "As a result of this, we are going to cancel and refund all current and future bookings and Kernow Christmas Market will take no further bookings for 2026.

"Any current bookings will be fully refunded and if any traders wish to continue to trade they must book direct with Pool Market."

Prior to the cancellation announcement, one stallholder, Ceilidh Hurrell, said she felt "let down" after paying £180 to trade at the event.

Hurrell, who runs Nails, Hair and More in Falmouth, paid for a pitch at the Christmas market, which formed part of the wider Winter Wonderland attraction with more stalls, Santa's grotto, an ice rink and fun fair.

She said she had expected a decorated venue to "entice people in for Christmas".

Instead, she said traders arrived to find no advertisement for the stallholders and no decorations.

"It was just an empty space. There was nothing to suggest that there's a market going on," Hurrell said.

Sammie Retallick, who attended with her partner on Saturday expecting a festive shopping experience, said they found "only about five stalls", as well as no decorations, Christmas music or lights.

Retallick said she felt sorry for traders who had invested money and time in the event.

"It's heartbreaking for them," she said.

Another trader claimed there were no signs directing visitors to the market area.

They added: "People turning up to the Winter Wonderland wouldn't have been aware we were even there.

"They've told us we're going to be part of this massive Winter Wonderland, 50-plus stalls, visitors of 2,500 people plus a day, then we get shoved in a dark corner of a warehouse."

Prior to the cancellation announcement, Rowland, who organises Winter Wonderland, said he took on the promotion of the market to help the Pool Market location.

"I thought it would be nice to help them," he said.

He said the AI images were "so easy to do" and gave a "rough idea" of what people could expect.

"You are never going to make it look exactly like the picture," he said.

Pool Market has been approached for comment.

Kernow Christmas Market said on Facebook the event was organised and operated by Pool Market, running alongside Cornwall Winter Wonderland.

It said: "We are a small, family run business that started many years ago here in Cornwall.

"This year, as an add on from Cornwalls Winter Wonderland we thought we would try and do a good deed and bring a little festive magic into Pool Market and for those who live locally in Cornwall.

"The agreement was always with Pool Market to do their bit and we do ours. We advertise it, book the stalls and they do the rest- such as signage, decorating and greeting the traders and helping them with queries.

"We are gutted, just as much as you all that things didn't go as planned."

It said Cornwall Winter Wonderland will remain open until 3 January and Rowlands' focus will remain "always remain on providing the very best experience for those who visit".

It added: "Entry is free, kindness is free, and we will always be grateful for those who continue to recognise the efforts, cost and dedication that goes on behind the scenes."

articles.title: Forwards and Bristol Sounds confirm headliners for summer 2027
articles.summary: Glastonbury, Forwards Festival and Bristol Sounds have all announced headliners for 2027.
articles.body:
We may be experiencing some chilly mornings and not many hours of daylight right now but festivals across the West have started releasing details of their headliners for summer 2027.

Forwards Festival revealed earlier that electronic duo Bicep will headline their event next year, with Bristol Sounds and Glastonbury announcing major acts as well.

Here are some of the bands and solo artists coming to events in the West next summer.

Fowards Festival will return to the Downs in Bristol for the sixth time in late August and has announced electronic duo Bicep as the first headliner.

Belfast-born and London-based duo Matt McBriar and Andy Ferguson, who will play on the Saturday, are returning to the city for the first time in five years.

Forwards will announce its second headliner later on Wednesday, with tickets going on general release on Monday.

Love Saves The Day returns to Ashton Court in Bristol in May, with Four Tet, Armand Van Helden and Damian Marley confirmed for the event.

The festival - set up in 2012 by Team Love, who are also behind Forwards - was previously held in Castle Park and Eastville Park.

The festival will also welcome Groove Armada, Shy FX, Oppidan and Kings of the Rollers, spanning house, techno, UK garage, reggae, jungle and drum and bass.

Tickets for the whole weekend are now on sale.

Bastille, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Roni Size & Reprazent have been announced as part of the first wave of acts scheduled to play Bristol Sounds next summer.

The event, beginning on 22 June, takes place at Lloyds Amphitheatre next to Bristol Harbour.

Tickets are already on sale while the rest of the line-up is yet to be announced.

The Bristol International Balloon Fiesta draws crowds of up to 500,000 to Ashton Court to watch the colourful hot air balloons during mass ascents and also evening nightglows.

The fiesta has confirmed it will be taking place from 13 to 15 August in 2027.

The 2027 event will celebrate the 60th anniversary of the Bristol Belle, the very first modern hot air balloon in Europe built by Don Cameron and members of the Bristol Gliding Club.

The event is free to attend but parking tickets are now on sale.

World of Music, Arts and Dance Festival (WOMAD) has been running for more than four decades and recently announced it will take place from 22-25 July 2027.

It used to be held at Charlton Park, near Malmesbury in Wiltshire, but for the first time this year it took place at Neston Park Estate near Corsham.

General admission tickets for the festival, co-founded by musician Peter Gabriel, will go on sale on 27 November.

Glastonbury Festival recently announced Harry Styles as one of the event's headliners, alongside Sam Fender and Billie Eilish - with Cher among the other stars on the bill.

Other acts on the line-up include Sombr, Sienna Spiro, Lily Allen, The Streets, Chase & Status, Kacey Musgraves, Primal Scream and breakout pop star Adéla.

Tickets for the festival sold out in just 42 minutes , with demand particularly high after the event took a year off in 2026.

The world-famous event will run from 23 to 27 June.

articles.title: Huge fly-tip in South Wigston grew undetected for several months
articles.summary: The council says the 20-tonne pile of rubbish was dumped over garden fences.
articles.body:
Two fly-tippers were able to dump huge amounts of household waste over their garden fences without being detected for several months, with the pile eventually reaching 20 tonnes.

It was spotted on land owned by a business in South Wigston, Leicestershire, earlier in the year.

However, due to the location of the fly-tip, it was not immediately visible to employees of the business, which Oadby and Wigston Borough Council said "allowed the offenders to act over several months".

The two individuals responsible were each issued with a £600 fixed penalty notice following an interview under caution, the authority added, while a third person was cautioned for their role in the offence.

Before the rubbish could be cleared, the council's environmental health officers worked with the business to gather evidence to prove who had been responsible.

The authority has not specified which business was affected by the fly-tipping, or from where the rubbish was sourced.

The council said it had also recently issued another £600 fine after a resident's waste was found in a lay-by off Gartree Road in Oadby.

They had not fly-tipped the rubbish themselves, the authority added, but had paid a rogue operator in good faith to take it away.

According to the council, residents have a duty of care for their waste until it is disposed of correctly and should ensure it is given to a licensed waste operator.

Councillor Samina Haq, leader of the council, said: "There is simply no excuse for fly-tipping. It damages our environment, costs money to clear up and is unfair on the overwhelming majority of residents and businesses who dispose of their waste responsibly.

"These successful cases send a clear message that we will investigate reports, gather evidence and take action against those responsible.

"Please continue to report fly-tipping whenever you see it and, if you pay someone to remove your waste, always make sure they are properly licensed."

articles.title: Blade Runner 2099: Hunter Schafer's series 'not just about AI'
articles.summary: Hunter Schafer and co-stars say the sci-fi TV show explores more than the idea of robotic consciousness.
articles.body:
"What does it mean to be human?" is a question that's always been at the heart of Blade Runner.

The first film in the series, released in 1982, depicted a technologically advanced yet dystopian version of Los Angeles in the then-distant future of 2019.

While the movie's flying cars haven't - quite - materialised yet in the real world, Blade Runner's themes of technological progress and the threats it poses feel just as relevant.

At least that's what the cast and crew of Blade Runner 2099, a new TV series set in the same universe, are hoping.

BBC Newsbeat spoke to stars Hunter Schafer, Lewis Gribben and Dimitri Abold, plus showrunner Silka Luisa, to ask why they think themes of artificial consciousness and existential threats still resonate.

The original Blade Runner, directed by Sir Ridley Scott, is considered a sci-fi classic that had a long-lasting influence on the genre.

It told the story of Detective Deckard, played by Harrison Ford, who hunted down synthetic humans known as replicants.

Schafer says her first exposure to the series was actually marketing for Blade Runner 2049 - the film sequel starring Ford and Ryan Gosling in 2017.

"I never thought I'd have the opportunity to make an addition to the world," she says.

"And so when that opportunity came along, I was quite thrilled."

Blade Runner 2099 is set 80 years after the original film, and portrays a Los Angeles where replicants have taken over.

Schafer plays Cora, a fugitive human forced to team up with replicant Olwen (played by Michelle Yeoh), as she tries to track down an artefact that could save humanity.

The series lands at a time when there are disagreements about the nature of the threat AI could pose to humans .

"I think it's particularly relevant right now, especially for the youth and young people who are inheriting a world that's asking a lot of the same questions that the show asks," says Schafer.

"I think that's timely and hopefully helpful to some degree."

But Blade Runner 2099 isn't "necessarily about just AI", says showrunner Luisa.

"It's this bigger question of what is the world going to be in 15 years and how can you plan for it?" she says.

The first Blade Runner also touched on themes of corporate greed and environmental damage, which are evident in the new series.

Luisa hopes the theme of a future that "is not going to be what you were promised" resonates with viewers today.

"The idea that you were born into a world and you thought you were expecting certain aspects of your life just to roll out," she says.

"That system is collapsing. And so what will be your place in whatever comes next?"

Blade Runner 2049 won awards and scored well with reviewers, but reports suggested it didn't hit box office targets.

This was partly blamed on marketing for the film trying to appeal more to existing fans than new ones - so what would the cast say to get younger viewers on board?

"It's just a very rich world," says Gribben, who plays Cora's younger brother Elias.

Gribben also points out that Blade Runner 2099, which employed "hundreds of artists and craftspeople" according to its makers, is a celebration of traditional film-making despite its themes.

"I think a lot of people crave human stories," he says.

"They crave new kind of worlds and new things.

"And I think studios will rely more on technology to make better-looking movies, but they won't have that soul."

Abold, who plays Cora's human ally Bebeto, says one of the show's key messages is about "the connections that you make".

"And the connections that you make are the foundation of humanity," he says.

"Because at the end of the day, all we have is ourselves and each other, right? And that's what feeds any human emotional experience."

Reviews for Blade Runner 2099 have been mostly positive, with a score of 72% on Rotten Tomatoes and an average of 65% on review aggregator Metacritic .

There was praise for the lead performances, the show's visual style and the way it updates the themes established in previous series entries.

The most common criticism was the show's pacing, with several critics describing it as a slow-burn and questioning whether Blade Runner worked as well off the big screen.

Schafer says she felt a lot of pressure when she signed up for the show

"It's something that we were all aware of when making this show," she says.

"Everybody who was working on this show loves Blade Runner.

"Most people who love film-making love Blade Runner, everybody brought their best to work.

Blade Runner 2099 is available on Prime Video from 25 November.

articles.title: Minnesota couple found guilty of $15 million healthcare fraud after billing insurers for fake treatments and unlicensed care, then spending proceeds on luxury cars and a mansion
articles.summary: A Minnesota couple has been found guilty of defrauding Medicare, Medicaid and private health insurers of more than $15 million through a medical billing
articles.body: A Minnesota couple has been found guilty of defrauding Medicare, Medicaid and private health insurers of more than $15 million through a medical billing scam that targeted elderly and vulnerable patients. Gabriel Adam Alexander Luthor, 40, and Elizabeth Christine Brown, 43, used their neurofeedback therapy company, Golden Victory Medical, to submit false claims for treatments that were never provided, services carried out by unlicensed technicians and appointments that were recorded as lasting longer than they did. A federal jury found both defendants guilty of six counts of wire fraud and one count of money laundering following an 11-day trial.How the couple carried out the $15 million Medicare fraud schemeAccording to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Luthor and Brown used their neurofeedback therapy company, Golden Victory Medical (GVM), to submit false medical bills to Medicare, Medicaid and other health insurers.The company billed for medical services that never took place, services performed by unlicensed technicians under the names of licensed professionals, and appointments falsely recorded as lasting longer than they actually did. On 586 days, GVM claimed in its insurance bills that its providers had spent more than 24 hours with patients.Couple established neurofeedback company to target elderly patientsThe scheme began in 2018, when Luthor and Brown, who were in a romantic relationship, lived in Las Vegas, Nevada. Brown held a master's degree in nursing and was licensed as an advanced practice registered nurse, commonly known as a nurse practitioner. Luthor had no medical training.In April 2018, Brown established GVM, and Luthor became a co-owner shortly afterwards. The couple identified potential patients, many of whom were elderly, confined to their homes or receiving hospice care. They arranged home visits by unlicensed neurofeedback technicians three times a week for treatment sessions.Couple disguised neurofeedback treatments to bill MedicareNeurofeedback is an investigational or alternative medical service that is not covered by Medicare or virtually any private health insurer. To obtain insurance payments, Luthor and Brown billed for other services, including neurobehavioural and psychological examinations.However, according to the DOJ, the vast majority of these billed services never took place, could not legally be performed by unlicensed and unsupervised technicians, or involved claims that significantly overstated the time spent with patients.The couple also failed to charge GVM patients their required co-payments, in violation of Medicare requirements. The DOJ said this meant many of the company's largely elderly patients did not notice or challenge the substantial amounts being billed to their insurance policies, although some patients raised complaints.Couple spent $15 million in fraudulent Medicare payments on a lavish lifestyleThrough the scheme, Luthor and Brown obtained more than $15 million from health insurers. The DOJ said they used the proceeds to substantially increase their standard of living, purchasing luxury vehicles and a mansion in Eden Prairie, Minnesota.In 2019, the couple moved from Las Vegas to Minnesota and bought a million-dollar mansion measuring 9,000 square feet. The property was purchased using proceeds from the fraud, and they relocated GVM's operational headquarters to the house.The couple also spent large sums on luxury travel to destinations including Vail and Miami, as well as regular visits to nightclubs where their bar bills exceeded $10,000, according to the DOJ.Auditor found only 9 per cent of the company's medical bills were supportedLuthor and Brown were repeatedly warned about their billing practices, but continued submitting false claims. A doctor who worked with Brown complained about her billing to the nursing boards in Nevada and Minnesota. A nurse practitioner also resigned and reported that GVM was submitting bills under her name for services she had not provided.A retired journalist separately complained that the company had billed insurers for medical services she had never received. The Centres for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) subsequently suspended Medicare payments to GVM over suspected fraud.An independent auditor found that only 9 per cent of GVM's billing codes were supported. The company's chief executive also warned Luthor and Brown that the billing problems could lead to serious legal consequences if they were not corrected. The couple fired the executive in retaliation, according to the DOJ. They also dismissed an outside billing contractor who warned them that the company was charging insurers too much for the services performed.How the $15 million Medicare fraud scheme unravelled and led to guilty verdictsThe DOJ said Luthor and Brown also laundered proceeds from their fraudulent activities by transferring approximately $350,000 through a series of bank accounts. The money was used to fund an investment in water-well drilling in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.In early 2023, law enforcement officers executed search warrants at the couple's Eden Prairie residence and GVM's clinic in Las Vegas. The company subsequently ceased operations.Luthor and Brown were each convicted of six counts of wire fraud and one count of money laundering. Wire fraud carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years, while money laundering carries a maximum sentence of 10 years.Announcing the verdict, US Attorney Daniel N. Rosen said: “The defendants took advantage of elderly patients and viewed them like an ATM, thinking they could just punch in the right codes, and money would come pouring out.”Rosen also commended the law enforcement agencies involved in the investigation, adding that his office would continue to pursue fraud cases. The investigation involved the US Postal Inspection Service, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Eden Prairie Police Department, the US Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General and the US Marshals Service.You use AI every day. articles.title: Two children among six dead after plane crash off Mississippi coast
articles.summary: Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, in the fuselage, the US Coast Guard said.
articles.body:
Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi on Tuesday, the US Coast Guard says.

The Cessna 210 was on its way from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware. Air traffic control lost touch with it at about 15:45 (21:45 GMT) and it later went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula and Horn Island, officials said.

Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, in the fuselage, said Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros.

Rescuers spent hours searching for the group and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane's cabin floating on the water, he said.

Cmdr Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard rescue mission co-ordinator, said: "While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency co-ordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families."

articles.title: Delhi man orders 4 silver coins on Amazon for Rs 5,996, gets 2 packets of rakhis instead; platform refunds money instead of replacement, consumer commission orders Rs 20,000 compensation
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A Delhi consumer commission has directed Amazon Seller Services Pvt Ltd to pay Rs 20,000 compensation to a customer who received two packets of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Delhi consumer commission has directed Amazon Seller Services Pvt Ltd to pay Rs 20,000 compensation to a customer who received two packets of rakhis instead of four silver coins worth Rs 5,996, holding the e-commerce platform guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practices.The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, South II, observed that Amazon should have arranged a replacement of the product instead of unilaterally refunding the amount paid by the customer.The order, passed on November 13, said the platform had also increased the price of the same product from Rs 5,996 to approximately Rs 30,000, which reflected its conduct towards an existing consumer.According to the complaint, Akshay Mittal, a Prime member, placed an order on November 10, 2023, for four 50-gram silver coins of 999 purity at an offer price of Rs 5,996.When the shipment was delivered on November 12, he opened the parcel in the presence of the delivery person and found two packets of rakhis instead of the silver coins.The delivery person allegedly refused to take back the wrong shipment or arrange a replacement. His supervisor asked Mittal to contact Amazon's customer support.Mittal subsequently approached the platform's customer care, which initially denied liability citing its non-returnable policy. Following further follow-ups, Amazon acknowledged the issue and registered a complaint on November 13.However, instead of delivering the ordered items or providing replacements, the company refunded Rs 5,996 on November 26.Mittal alleged that by then Amazon had increased the listing price of the same product to around Rs 30,000, making it unavailable at the original offer price and causing him a differential loss of approximately Rs 24,000.He approached the commission seeking fulfilment of the original order, compensation of Rs 10 lakh and litigation costs.Amazon did not appear before the commission despite notice and was proceeded against ex parte in August 2025.The other respondents, Arihant Gems & Jewels and its proprietor Vikas Jain, argued that Mittal had already received a full refund while retaining the delivered goods. They also questioned the absence of photographic or video evidence proving that the parcel contained a different product.However, the commission noted that Mittal had submitted photographs showing the Amazon-labelled delivery packaging, along with two packets of fancy rakhis, a handwritten note bearing his name and the date November 26, 2023, as well as screenshots of his communication with customer care.Referring to Section 6(1) of the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, the commission observed that e-commerce entities were liable for unfair trade practices and sellers were required to fulfil their obligations concerning the delivery of goods and services.It further noted that Mittal had never sought a refund and that Amazon should have provided a replacement for the product originally ordered.Holding Amazon guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practices, the commission directed it to pay Rs 20,000 as compensation for mental harassment and physical inconvenience.The amount must be paid within 60 days of the order, failing which it will attract interest at 9%.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Bhopal car owner loses consumer case as commission upholds Rs 1 lakh insurance payout against Rs 8.22 lakh repair estimate
articles.summary: BHOPAL: A car swept away by a strong current of rainwater, partially submerged and rendered unusable ended up triggering a consumer dispute over an Rs
articles.body: BHOPAL: A car swept away by a strong current of rainwater, partially submerged and rendered unusable ended up triggering a consumer dispute over an Rs 8.22 lakh repair estimate and an insurance settlement of just Rs 1 lakh.The car owner, who alleged that the insurer had arbitrarily rejected a major part of his claim and the authorised workshop had charged him separately for repairs, has lost his case before the Gwalior District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission.Dismissing the complaint, the commission held that the owner had failed to produce technical or expert evidence establishing that all the defects in his vehicle were caused by the flooding. It also found no sufficient reason to reject the assessment of the insurance company's independent surveyor.The case involved Ajeet Singh Tomar, 44, who had insured his car, registration number MP-07-CJ-2266, with Universal Sompo General Insurance Company. The complaint was also filed against Prem Motors Pvt Ltd's Nexa service centre in Gwalior.According to the complaint, the incident occurred during the insurance period when the car was parked outside his residence. Following sudden rainfall and waterlogging, the vehicle was caught in a strong current and swept away. It was partially submerged, allowing water and mud to enter several parts of the vehicle and leaving it in a non-functional condition.The car was subsequently towed to Prem Motors' service centre, where the workshop estimated the repair cost at Rs 8,22,438.However, the insurance company, after arranging an inspection by an independent surveyor, approved only Rs 1,00,291 towards the damage. The insurer maintained that several components claimed to have been damaged were either not affected by waterlogging or were not covered under the policy.In a communication dated December 15, 2025, the insurer specifically disputed damage to components such as the clutch plate, speakers and headlight.Tomar alleged that the insurer had failed to honour the claim despite the vehicle suffering extensive damage in the incident. He further claimed that the workshop collected Rs 20,676 from him for replacing the clutch plate and other components, even though he believed the repairs should have been covered by the insurance claim.The dispute did not end with the repairs. On September 22, 2025, while returning from Mathura, Tomar reportedly encountered a battery-related problem with the car. He approached a local mechanic, who charged him Rs 1,475. The mechanic allegedly told him that nuts and bolts connected to the lithium battery had been left loose during the earlier repair work.Tomar accused the workshop of incomplete repairs and alleged that both the insurer and the service centre had indulged in deficiency of service and unfair trade practices. He sought complete repairs, a refund of Rs 20,676 and compensation for mental agony.Universal Sompo maintained that the claim had been assessed by an independent licensed surveyor and settled according to the admissible damage. It argued that the defects excluded from the claim did not match the circumstances of the reported incident and were outside the policy's coverage.Prem Motors, meanwhile, maintained that it had carried out repairs approved by the insurance company and undertaken the remaining work with the owner's consent. The commission examined the documentary evidence and affidavits before concluding that the owner's allegations were not supported by sufficient technical evidence. It observed that he had failed to establish that all the defects for which he sought reimbursement had resulted solely from the vehicle being partially submerged in floodwater.It also found no adequate grounds to disbelieve the independent surveyor's assessment, on the basis of which the insurer had approved the claim of Rs 1,00,291.On the additional Rs 20,676 collected by the workshop, the commission noted that there was no evidence establishing that the clutch plate and other components were part of the damage assessed by the surveyor. It held that charging separately for repairs beyond the approved estimate could not, by itself, establish deficiency in service.The commission, headed by president Rajendra Prasad Sharma, dismissed the complaint on November 13, 2026, and directed both sides to bear their own litigation expenses.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bhopal | Silver Rate in Bhopal | Bank Holidays in Bhopal | Public Holidays in Bhopal | Petrol Price in Bhopal | Diesel Price in Bhopal | CNG Price in Bhopal | LPG Price in BhopalStay updated with the latest Bhopal news. articles.summary: Tickets for Kendal Calling are going back on sale on Thursday now the line-up has been revealed.

The Chemical Brothers and Blossoms have been announced as headliners for Kendal Calling 2027.

The remaining headline acts for the four-day festival at Lowther Deer Park, in Cumbria, have also been revealed as Black Eyed Peas and Jamie T.

The festival will take place from Thursday 29 July until Sunday 1 August and will feature more than 100 acts, including musicians and comedians.

Some festival tickets were made available earlier in the year but a new batch will be put on sale in the coming days.

Indie rock bands The Wombats, James and Razorlight will also be performing as well as British rapper Dizzee Rascal and singer-songwriter Declan McKenna.

Other notable acts include DMA's, The Lottery Winners, The K's La Roux and Pale Waves.

Next year's event will mark the 22nd Kendal Calling festival, which had just 900 attendees in its first year.

More than 40,000 people now attend the festival each year.

articles.title: Rescuers search for dozens trapped in flooded Indonesia gold mine
articles.summary: Police say 26 workers are yet to be rescued from a mine that flooded when a nearby river overflowed after heavy rain.
articles.body:
Rescuers are searching for dozens of workers feared trapped in a flooded unauthorised mine in Indonesia’s West Java province, police and authorities said.

The open-pit gold mine in Java’s Bogor district was flooded when a nearby river overflowed after a torrential downpour on Monday, trapping the miners, police said on Wednesday.

“As of now, there were 26 people who have yet to be evacuated,” said West Java police spokesman Hendra Rochmawan in a statement.

The Jakarta Search and Rescue Office said the workers were stuck in a 100-metre (328-foot) deep mine. Access ⁠was narrow, and the terrain was slippery and dark, the agency added, giving no details of the size of the rescue operation or any progress made towards reaching the trapped miners.

“We are coordinating with all search and rescue personnel involved in the operation to monitor water conditions and assess access to the mine shaft,” Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in ⁠a statement.

“The depth of the shaft, narrow ⁠access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely.”

The mine is located in the Pongkor area of Bogor, a mountainous area 60km south of the capital Jakarta, where state miner ⁠Antam runs gold-mining operations.

Small-scale and unauthorised mining ‌has often led to accidents in resource-rich Indonesia, where mineral resources are located in remote areas in conditions difficult for authorities to regulate .

Authorities closed ‌about ‌30 gold mine pits last week in a separate area in Bogor, news website Detik reported.

articles.title: From stargazing to space: Pakistan watches its first astronaut take flight
articles.summary: Students and stargazers packed SUPARCO’s auditorium before dawn to watch Zeeshan Ali reach orbit on a Chinese rocket.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan — It was 5:18am (00:18 GMT) on Wednesday, before dawn in a chilly Islamabad. On the screen at the front of the auditorium, a Chinese rocket carrying Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, Pakistan’s first astronaut, rose on a column of orange flames.

As the rocket lifted off, Pakistan’s national anthem began. The audience, which had been slouching in their seats, rose row by row and sang along.

While many took out their phones to record the historic moment, Zainab Abbasi’s eyes remained fixed on the giant screen.

“I had my phone out to record it on video, but I was so caught up in the moment that I forgot to record, and I was just standing there with my phone closed,” Abbasi, 21, told Al Jazeera.

A second-year undergraduate student of physics and astronomy at the National University of Sciences and Technology (NUST), Abbasi was with her friends in the auditorium at the headquarters of the Pakistan Space & Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO).

As the rocket climbed higher, the hall erupted in applause and chants of “Pakistan Zindabad” (“Long live Pakistan”).

The Long March-2F rocket lifted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northwest China, carrying Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi, alongside Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan Air Force pilot.

But within two minutes of liftoff, the hall fell silent. No one spoke. Faces across the rows were tense. On the screen, the rocket had shrunk to a dot.

“There was, I think, anticipation and also, for me specifically, a sort of, you know, underlying anxiety,” Abbasi told Al Jazeera.

On January 28, 1986, the US space shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff, killing all seven crew members.

About 10 minutes after Wednesday’s launch, the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft separated from the rocket and entered orbit, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA).

The silence lasted several minutes, until one of the hosts congratulated the audience on a successful launch. People got up, greeted one another or headed for the doors.

A few hours later, CMSA and SUPARCO confirmed that the spacecraft had docked at China’s Tiangong space station at 8:56am (03:56 GMT). The crew were expected to enter the station at about 11:45am (06:45 GMT).

The auditorium had been packed by 5am (00:00 GMT). Those unable to find a seat sat on the floor or stood along the walls.

Tayyaba Riaz, a final-year mathematics student at NUST, said every seat was taken when she arrived at about 4:20am (23:20 GMT Tuesday). Originally from Chitral in Pakistan’s northwest, she lives in a university hostel.

When she asked hostel authorities to leave early in the morning, she said they asked where she was going. “I was like, ‘I am going to witness a history,’” she said, giggling.

Many in the auditorium held glossy cards bearing Ali’s portrait in a spacesuit and the words “Pakistan’s First Manned Space Mission”. Paper flags of Pakistan and China rested on laps, while green and white balloons lined the stage.

The screen carried a livestream of the launch. There was a brief moment of hilarity when, just before liftoff, a YouTube advertisement appeared, causing mild panic that the critical moment might be missed.

Abbasi, the second-year student, had been at SUPARCO since 2am (21:00 GMT Tuesday). She lives 40km (25 miles) away and had left home at 7pm (14:00 GMT) on Tuesday to spend the night at her aunt’s house nearby.

She is a member of PakAstronomers, a group of amateur astronomers in Islamabad. Her interest in astronomy began around 2018, when she was 13, after the cartoon series Beyblade introduced her to constellations.

Her family, particularly her father, has always supported her, even if they do not always understand her passion, she said.

“When I was a child and interested in space, becoming an astronaut felt like a far-off dream only available to a child in America and not in Pakistan,” she said.

Ahzam Farooq, a physics undergraduate at NUST and vice president of the society, used to wake at 3am to watch rocket launches.

“My parents used to ask, ‘What is there in this?’ like it will never be us,” he said.

Adan Athar, a second-year space sciences student at the Institute of Space Technology (IST) in Islamabad, is from Faisalabad and a founding member of the Faisalabad Astronomical Society.

She told Al Jazeera she was the first in her family to take an interest in space.

“Yes, they were very supportive, and they think I will be the next astronaut,” she said with a shy smile.

But it is not only Pakistan’s youth following Ali’s journey.

Saif-ul-Islam Qureshi, a 72-year-old electronics engineer, has been watching the sky for at least 50 years.

“I was 12 years old when I started this hobby with my small binocular, and then my first observation was the Big Dipper in the sky,” he told Al Jazeera.

The Big Dipper is a group of seven bright stars whose two end stars point towards the North Star.

Qureshi helped found PakAstronomers, the group Abbasi belongs to. It was initially called the Pakistan Astronomy Society.

Its members took astronomy to schools, colleges, universities and public parks. Many people did not know planets could be seen with the naked eye, he said.

Over the past decade, however, that had changed. Even small children were now well informed.

“We were sensing that a storm was building. A storm is building, and a storm in a positive sense,” he said.

In a speech before the launch, SUPARCO chairman Muhammad Yousaf Khan said Pakistan was setting its sights further ahead.

“Our ambition is beyond just this launch. Our commitment is to reach the moon by 2035,” he said.

Speaking to Al Jazeera afterwards, Khan said the first step would be a lunar rover, due to fly in 2028.

“If the Chinese people have reached here, there is no shortcoming in us. I believe one day, we too will reach that stage, if we keep moving step by step,” Khan told Al Jazeera.

Farooq, the NUST physics undergraduate, said collaboration with China could help Pakistan avoid having to build its space capabilities from scratch.

“If we have this collaboration, I think it’s good that we can use the already built-up platforms of China and utilise them to do something further. By making our own satellites, and through our own astronauts, we can go towards some further research,” he told Al Jazeera.

For Qureishi, the veteran astronomer, that excitement for the future climaxed when Ali took off. That moment, he said, was about much more than Ali.

“It is not Zeeshan [in the astronaut’s seat]. It is Pakistan’s young generation sitting there,” he said.
